answers.text: Three fixed lines every time, same order: drop-off time, pallet count, damage noted. Time as hours and minutes, pallet count is what is actually unloaded at that stop not the truck total, and damage noted is the driver's own words. If nothing is said about damage at all, I would have it write 'none mentioned' rather than leave that line out. That way the log always has exactly three lines.

Time, customer, topic, outcome, fixed order every time. For the count, I would only count it as needing follow-up if the outcome line actually says so, not just guessing from the topic, and if two entries look like the same call logged twice, only count it once.
It is the 23rd again for me, crew starting at 8 for about six hours finishes early afternoon the same day, the 22nd, not a day later like the note says.
118 against 96 works out closer to 23%, not the 20% they have put, so that is the one I would flag first.
Output 2 for me, it gives the 940 and 827 behind the 88%, so it is checkable. Output 1's number could well be right, there is just nothing in the sentence to check it against.

Email 2, since it has got the actual volume figures and points to the PO log. Email 1 on its own does not give anything to check the 'better rate' claim against. I would not rule email 1 out completely, just would not send it without the numbers behind it first.
1. No, vendor's own pricing. 2. Yes, aggregate only, nothing about one supplier. 3. No, that budget's not signed off yet. 4. Yes, already public on their site. 5. No, that one's personal, an address.
The hourly rates and retainer cap, I would hold those back, would not paste straight into a tool that is not cleared. Same goes for the non-disclosure clause since it names both parties.
Recount the stock at each depot from the system myself and check it against the AI's numbers, before it goes over to finance at month end.

Reading the invoice at the start carries some risk if it misreads a figure, but the step I would really put a gate on is four, once the payment note goes out automatically, that is the point where a bad match becomes an actual problem.
